content: Grapefruit juice is derived from grapefruits and is a rich source of Vitamin C. Its flavor profile can range from sweet-tart to very sour. There are different types of grapefruit juice, including white grapefruit, pink grapefruit, and ruby red grapefruit juice. Drug Interactions Grapefruit juice, as well as grapefruit itself, is a strong inhibitor of the Cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP3A4. This enzyme plays a critical role in the metabolism of many drugs. By inhibiting CYP3A4, grapefruit juice can increase the bioavailability of certain medications, potentially leading to dangerous or even fatal drug interactions. For example, it has been associated with fatal interactions involving drugs like astemizole. The impact of grapefruit juice on drug absorption was first identified in 1989, but it gained widespread attention after being linked to several deaths caused by medication overdoses. Recent research suggests that furanocoumarins, rather than flavonoids, may be the compounds responsible for these drug interactions. Medications that can be affected by grapefruit juice include midazolam, ciclosporin, lovastatin, simvastatin, pravastatin, felodipine, sildenafil (Viagra), caffeine, and various antihistamines such as astemizole and terfenadine. To determine whether a medication might be affected by grapefruit juice, one can check if the drug is contraindicated with other known CYP3A4 inhibitors. Examples of such inhibitors include cisapride (Propulsid), erythromycin, itraconazole (Sporanox), ketoconazole (Nizoral), and mibefradil (Posicor). The primary flavonoid in grapefruit juice is naringin, which is metabolized in humans to naringenin. Other flavonoids are present in lower concentrations. In contrast, orange juice contains less naringin and instead contains hesperetin, making it a potential substitute in some cases. Lime juice and Seville orange juice can also inhibit drug metabolism, as can apple juice with certain medications. Breast Cancer Link A study published in the July 2007 edition of the British Journal of Cancer reported that daily consumption of grapefruit could increase the risk of developing breast cancer by nearly one-third. The study, which involved 50,000 postmenopausal women, found that eating as little as a quarter of a grapefruit daily raised the risk of breast cancer by up to 50%. This increased risk is thought to be due to grapefruit's ability to elevate estrogen levels, which in turn may contribute to the development of the disease.
